steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react' here

// No other code yet
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: Import statement for React
Import statement for useState
Both imported from 'react'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState from 'react'. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement needs adjustment. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React and useState from 'react' to proceed.

steps.title: Import useEffect and useRef from 'react'
steps.instruction: Add an import statement to bring in the useEffect and useRef hooks from the 'react' package. Place it after the existing import line.
steps.hint: Use the same import syntax as before, but specify both useEffect and useRef from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing multiple hooks from 'react'
import { useState, useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have two import statements: one for React and useState, and another for useEffect and useRef.
successCriteria: The import statement includes both useEffect and useRef from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported both useEffect and useRef. These hooks are essential for managing side effects and mutable references in React components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both useEffect and useRef from 'react' in a single import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import both useEffect and useRef from the 'react' package. Check the syntax for importing multiple named exports.

steps.title: Create the main component function
steps.instruction: Create a function component named MemoryLeakHunt that returns JSX.Element. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component function that returns a JSX element. For TypeScript, you can specify the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A component function named MemoryLeakHunt is defined with proper TypeScript typing.
successCriteria:
The component should be named MemoryLeakHunt, return JSX.Element, and have a function body that returns a JSX element (even if it's just a placeholder like
).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the MemoryLeakHunt component function with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the component is named exactly 'MemoryLeakHunt' and returns JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you've defined a function named MemoryLeakHunt that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize state for counter
steps.instruction: Inside your MemoryLeakHunt component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 0. Remember to destructure the array to get both the state variable and its setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a counter state
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a 'count' state variable initialized to 0, ready to be used in the UI and updated by event handlers.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that creates a 'count' variable and its setter, with an initial value of 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the count state variable. This gives us a numeric value we can display and update throughout our memory leak demonstration.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your useState implementation. Make sure you're creating a 'count' variable with an initial value of 0, and destructuring both the value and setter from the useState return array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count state hasn't been properly initialized. Remember to use useState with an initial value of 0 and destructure the result into 'count' and its setter function.

steps.title: Initialize state for timer active status
steps.instruction: Inside the MemoryLeakHunt component, use the useState hook to create a new state variable named 'isTimerActive' and initialize it to false. Remember to use TypeScript generics to specify the type as boolean.
steps.hint: You'll need to call useState<boolean>(false) and destructure the returned array into a variable and setter, similar to how you created the 'count' state.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two state variables: 'count' (number) and 'isTimerActive' (boolean).
successCriteria: State variable named 'isTimerActive' is declared
It uses useState<boolean>(false)
It's properly destructured into variable and setter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a boolean state variable to track whether the timer is active. This will be essential for controlling the timer's lifecycle.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you specify the type as boolean with useState<boolean>? Did you initialize it to false?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on creating just this one state variable. Use useState<boolean>(false) to create a boolean state variable named 'isTimerActive'.

steps.title: Create a ref for interval ID
steps.instruction: Inside your MemoryLeakHunt component, use the useRef hook to create a mutable reference called intervalRef. Initialize it with null and specify its type as NodeJS.Timeout | null.
steps.hint: Call useRef<Type>(initialValue) to create a ref. The type should be NodeJS.Timeout | null since setInterval returns a NodeJS.Timeout.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a ref for an interval ID
const intervalRef = useRef<NodeJS.Timeout | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a ref named intervalRef that can hold the interval ID for cleanup later.
successCriteria: The code must include a call to useRef with the correct type NodeJS.Timeout | null and initial value null, assigned to a variable named intervalRef.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a ref to store the interval ID. This will allow us to clear the interval properly and prevent memory leaks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track with creating a ref, but check the type annotation and initial value. It should be useRef<NodeJS.Timeout | null>(null).
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on creating a ref specifically for the interval ID. Use the useRef hook with the correct type and initial value.

steps.title: Define the startTimer handler
steps.instruction: Define a function named startTimer inside your MemoryLeakHunt component. This function should set isTimerActive to true and start an interval that increments the count state every second.
steps.hint: Use setInterval to create a recurring function call. Store the interval ID in the intervalRef.current property. Remember to update the isTimerActive state.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a startTimer function that sets isTimerActive to true and creates an interval that increments count every second.
successCriteria: Function named startTimer is defined
Function sets isTimerActive to true
Function uses setInterval to increment count
Interval ID is stored in intervalRef.current
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the startTimer handler that activates the timer and increments the counter.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check if you're: 1) setting isTimerActive to true, 2) using setInterval correctly, and 3) storing the interval ID in intervalRef.current.
steps.feedbackWrong: The startTimer function isn't defined correctly. Make sure you create a function that sets isTimerActive to true and starts an interval that increments count every second.

steps.title: Define the stopTimer handler
steps.instruction: Inside your MemoryLeakHunt component, define a function called stopTimer that clears the interval stored in intervalRef and sets isTimerActive to false.
steps.hint: Use the clearInterval function with intervalRef.current, then call setIsTimerActive with false.
steps.expectedOutcome: A stopTimer function that properly cleans up the interval and updates the timer state.
successCriteria:
The stopTimer function must:
1. Check if intervalRef.current exists
2. Call clearInterval with intervalRef.current
3. Set intervalRef.current to null
4. Call setIsTimerActive with false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the stopTimer handler that properly clears the interval and updates the timer state. This is crucial for preventing memory leaks by cleaning up the interval when it's no longer needed.
steps.feedbackPartial:
You're on the right track, but your stopTimer function is missing some important parts. Make sure to:
1. Check if intervalRef.current exists before clearing it
2. Set intervalRef.current to null after clearing
3. Update isTimerActive state to false

Try adding the missing pieces to ensure proper cleanup.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The stopTimer function doesn't seem to be defined correctly. You need to create a function called stopTimer that:
1. Clears the interval stored in intervalRef.current
2. Sets intervalRef.current to null
3. Updates isTimerActive state to false

Look at the analogous example for guidance on the proper structure.

steps.title: Add useEffect for timer cleanup
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook that returns a cleanup function to clear the interval when the component unmounts.
steps.hint: Use useEffect with an empty dependency array ([]). Inside the effect, return a function that calls clearInterval with intervalRef.current.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a useEffect hook that ensures the interval is cleared when the component unmounts, preventing memory leaks.
successCriteria: A useEffect hook is added
The effect has an empty dependency array []
The effect returns a cleanup function
The cleanup function checks intervalRef.current and calls clearInterval
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a cleanup effect that will clear the interval when the component unmounts, preventing potential memory leaks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your useEffect has an empty dependency array and returns a cleanup function that clears the interval.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding a useEffect hook with an empty dependency array that returns a function to clear the interval. This ensures cleanup when the component unmounts.

steps.title: Create the component structure
steps.instruction: Return a div container with appropriate className for the main component structure.
steps.hint: Add a div element with a descriptive className inside the component's return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a div element with a descriptive className that will serve as the main container.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element
The div has a className attribute
The className is descriptive (e.g., 'memory-leak-hunt')
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main container structure for your component with a descriptive className.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added a className to the div element and that it's descriptive.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div element with a className attribute. Check that you've added the div inside the return statement.

steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add two paragraph elements to display the current count value and timer status.
steps.hint: Use JSX curly braces to embed the state values: {count} and {isTimerActive}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will show the current counter value and whether the timer is active in the UI.

element displaying count

steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added UI elements to display the current counter value and timer status. This makes the state visible to users.

steps.feedbackWrong: The UI doesn't yet display the state values. Add two paragraph elements inside the div that show {count} and {isTimerActive}.

steps.title: Add timer control buttons with click handlers
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add two button elements: one with text 'Start Timer' that calls startTimer when clicked, and another with text 'Stop Timer' that calls stopTimer when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on each button to connect them to the handler functions that were defined in previous steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two interactive buttons that control the timer when clicked.
successCriteria: The code must include two button elements inside the return statement, each with appropriate text and onClick handlers that call the existing startTimer and stopTimer functions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the timer control buttons with proper click handlers. The UI now has interactive elements to start and stop the timer.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be an issue with the button setup. Make sure you have both buttons with the correct text ('Start Timer' and 'Stop Timer') and that each onClick handler calls the corresponding function (startTimer for the first button, stopTimer for the second).
steps.feedbackWrong: The buttons aren't properly set up. You need to add two button elements inside the return statement, each with onClick handlers that call the existing startTimer and stopTimer functions. Check that the button text matches the expected labels.
